claim: Old age is the greatest risk factor for dementia.
source: Because old age is the greatest risk factor for dementia, a successful therapy will require an understanding of the physiological changes that occur in the brain with aging.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific citation, representing accepted scientific consensus.

claim: CMS121 and J147 reduced cognitive decline in rapidly aging SAMP8 mice when administered late in life.
source: CMS121 and J147 reduced cognitive decline as well as metabolic and transcriptional markers of aging in the brain when administered to rapidly aging SAMP8 mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral testing data presented in Figure 2 showing improvements in elevated plus maze and Barnes maze performance.

claim: CMS121 and J147 reduced metabolic markers of aging in the brain of SAMP8 mice.
source: CMS121 and J147 reduced cognitive decline as well as metabolic and transcriptional markers of aging in the brain when administered to rapidly aging SAMP8 mice.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic profiling data showing preservation of TCA cycle metabolites and other metabolic changes presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: CMS121 and J147 reduced transcriptional markers of aging in the brain of SAMP8 mice.
source: CMS121 and J147 reduced cognitive decline as well as metabolic and transcriptional markers of aging in the brain when administered to rapidly aging SAMP8 mice.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing prevention of age-related transcriptomic changes presented in Figure 1.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 preserved mitochondrial homeostasis by regulating acetyl-CoA metabolism.
source: Both compounds preserved mitochondrial homeostasis by regulating acetyl-coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including metabolomic data, network analysis, and direct measurement of acetyl-CoA levels in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in cell culture via the inhibition of ACC1.
source: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in cell culture and mice via the inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), resulting in neuroprotection and increased acetylation of histone H3K9 in SAMP8 mice, a site linked to memory enhancement.
evidence: This is supported by direct measurements of acetyl-CoA levels and ACC1 phosphorylation in cell culture shown in Figure 6.

claim: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in mice via the inhibition of ACC1.
source: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in cell culture and mice via the inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), resulting in neuroprotection and increased acetylation of histone H3K9 in SAMP8 mice, a site linked to memory enhancement.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of acetyl-CoA levels and ACC1 phosphorylation in SAMP8 mouse brains shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: CMS121 and J147 increased acetylation of histone H3K9 in SAMP8 mice.
source: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in cell culture and mice via the inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), resulting in neuroprotection and increased acetylation of histone H3K9 in SAMP8 mice, a site linked to memory enhancement.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased H3K9 acetylation in SAMP8 cortex presented in Figure 6C.

claim: Histone H3K9 is a site linked to memory enhancement.
source: CMS121 and J147 increased the levels of acetyl-CoA in cell culture and mice via the inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), resulting in neuroprotection and increased acetylation of histone H3K9 in SAMP8 mice, a site linked to memory enhancement.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mews et al., 2017 and Fischer et al., 2007 in the text.

claim: Targeting specific metabolic aspects of the aging brain could result in treatments for dementia.
source: These data show that targeting specific metabolic aspects of the aging brain could result in treatments for dementia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that compounds targeting acetyl-CoA metabolism improve cognitive function.

claim: Age is the greatest risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
source: Age is the greatest risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge representing scientific consensus.

claim: A decline in cerebral glucose metabolism precedes the pathology and symptoms of AD.
source: Clinical evidence shows that a decline in cerebral glucose metabolism (hypometabolism) precedes the pathology and symptoms of AD and is more severe than that observed in normal aging (Costantini et al., 2008; Cunnane et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Cerebral glucose hypometabolism in AD is more severe than that observed in normal aging.
source: Clinical evidence shows that a decline in cerebral glucose metabolism (hypometabolism) precedes the pathology and symptoms of AD and is more severe than that observed in normal aging (Costantini et al., 2008; Cunnane et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: A failure to supply cells with adequate energy contributes to the neuropathological cascade in both aging and age-associated dementias such as AD.
source: Given that energy production from glucose supports the majority of brain activity as well as the maintenance of cellular homeostasis, it is likely that a failure to supply cells with adequate energy contributes to the neuropathological cascade in both aging and age-associated dementias such as AD (Caldwell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Caldwell et al., 2015.

claim: A number of mitochondrial-dependent functions are impaired during aging and AD.
source: Not surprisingly, a number of mitochondrial-dependent functions are found to be impaired during aging and AD (Caldwell et al., 2015; Chan, 2006; Currais, 2015a; Lin and Beal, 2006; Onyango et al., 2016; Swerdlow and Khan, 2004; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to seven published studies.

claim: Brain mitochondrial dysfunction has been hypothesized to be responsible for the pathological hallmarks of AD.
source: In fact, brain mitochondrial dysfunction has been hypothesized to be responsible for the pathological hallmarks of AD (Swerdlow and Khan, 2004; Yin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two published studies.

claim: J147 is active in transgenic AD animal models.
source: J147 is active in transgenic AD animal models (Chen et al., 2011; Daugherty et al., 2017; Prior et al., 2013; Prior et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to four published studies.

claim: J147 enhances memory in rapidly aging SAMP8 mice when administered early in life.
source: It enhances memory and prevents some aspects of aging in rapidly aging (15 month median lifespan) senescence-accelerated prone 8 (SAMP8) mice when administered early in life (Currais et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Currais et al., 2015b.

claim: J147 prevents some aspects of aging in rapidly aging SAMP8 mice when administered early in life.
source: It enhances memory and prevents some aspects of aging in rapidly aging (15 month median lifespan) senescence-accelerated prone 8 (SAMP8) mice when administered early in life (Currais et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Currais et al., 2015b.

claim: SAMP8 mice have a median lifespan of 15 months.
source: It enhances memory and prevents some aspects of aging in rapidly aging (15 month median lifespan) senescence-accelerated prone 8 (SAMP8) mice when administered early in life (Currais et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is stated as a factual characteristic of the SAMP8 mouse model.

claim: CMS121 is a more potent derivative of the flavonol fisetin that maintains most of its biological properties.
source: CMS121 is a more potent derivative of the flavonol fisetin that maintains most of its biological properties (Chiruta et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chiruta et al., 2012.

claim: Fisetin is able to ameliorate some aspects of aging in SAMP8 mice.
source: CMS121 is not as well studied as J147, but we have recently shown that fisetin is able to ameliorate some aspects of aging in SAMP8 mice (Currais et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Currais et al., 2018.

claim: The target of J147 is the alpha subunit of ATP synthase.
source: The target of J147 is the alpha subunit of ATP synthase, which engages a neuroprotective response involving the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Goldberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2018.

claim: J147 binding to ATP synthase engages a neuroprotective response involving the activation of AMPK.
source: The target of J147 is the alpha subunit of ATP synthase, which engages a neuroprotective response involving the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Goldberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2018.

claim: ATP synthase is an anti-aging target in C. elegans.
source: ATP synthase is an anti-aging target in C. elegans (Chin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chin et al., 2014.

claim: CMS121 does not target ATP synthase.
source: We have ruled out that CMS121 also targets ATP synthase (unpublished data), and its molecular targets are currently under investigation.
evidence: This is based on unpublished experimental data from the authors.

claim: There was a clear distinction in the variation of the transcriptome between 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice.
source: Principle component analysis (PCA) showed a clear distinction in the variation of the transcriptome between the 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 groups, indicating that aging has a strong effect on gene expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Aging has a strong effect on gene expression in SAMP8 mice.
source: Principle component analysis (PCA) showed a clear distinction in the variation of the transcriptome between the 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 groups, indicating that aging has a strong effect on gene expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference from the PCA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 treated groups presented a distribution in the two major principle components that was closer to the 9 months old mice.
source: Importantly, both compound-treated groups presented a distribution in the two major principle components (PCs) that was closer to the 9 months old mice, suggesting that the compounds can prevent transcriptomic changes that take place with aging (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CMS121 and J147 can prevent transcriptomic changes that take place with aging.
source: Importantly, both compound-treated groups presented a distribution in the two major principle components (PCs) that was closer to the 9 months old mice, suggesting that the compounds can prevent transcriptomic changes that take place with aging (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference from the PCA data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was a significant age-associated drift in gene expression between 9 and 13 months in SAMP8 mice.
source: Transcriptomic drift analysis, a method to characterize the aging process that measures changes in gene expression at a global level (Rangaraju et al., 2015), showed a significant age-associated drift in gene expression between 9 and 13 months that was also suppressed by both compounds (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic drift analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The age-associated drift in gene expression was suppressed by both CMS121 and J147.
source: Transcriptomic drift analysis, a method to characterize the aging process that measures changes in gene expression at a global level (Rangaraju et al., 2015), showed a significant age-associated drift in gene expression between 9 and 13 months that was also suppressed by both compounds (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic drift analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 485 differently expressed genes were found between the 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice.
source: 485 differently expressed (DE) genes were found between the 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 684 DE genes were detected between the 13 months and 13 months+CMS121 SAMP8 mice.
source: 684 and 34 DE genes were detected between the 13 months and 13 months+CMS121 and 13 months+J147 SAMP8 mice, respectively (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 34 DE genes were detected between the 13 months and 13 months+J147 SAMP8 mice.
source: 684 and 34 DE genes were detected between the 13 months and 13 months+CMS121 and 13 months+J147 SAMP8 mice, respectively (Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: For all of the DE genes that overlap between aging and compound treatment, the age-dependent changes in expression were prevented by the compounds.
source: For all of the DE genes that overlap between aging and compound treatment (shared DE genes), the age-dependent changes in expression were prevented by the compounds (Figure 1C, middle set of graphs).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The age-dependent alterations in most DE genes specific for each comparison follow the same trend of prevention by the compounds.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the DE genes that are specific for each comparison (those that do not overlap) also shows that the age-dependent alterations in most of these DE genes follow the same trend of prevention by the compounds.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 reduce aging at the level of the transcriptome in the hippocampus of SAMP8 mice when administered at a late stage of the aging process.
source: Thus, these data provide evidence that both compounds reduce aging at the level of the transcriptome in the hippocampus of SAMP8 mice when administered at a late stage of the aging process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptomic data presented in Figure 1.

claim: There was a decline in average velocity between the 9 and 13 months SAMP8 mice.
source: Assessment of spontaneous behavior in the open field assay showed only a decline in average velocity between the 9 and 13 months SAMP8 mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CMS121 and J147 had no effect on average velocity in SAMP8 mice.
source: The compounds had no effect on this parameter or on body weights (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CMS121 and J147 had no effect on body weights in SAMP8 mice.
source: The compounds had no effect on this parameter or on body weights (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: 13 months old SAMP8 mice spent significantly more time in the open arms of the elevated plus maze compared to 9 months old SAMP8 mice.
source: 13 months old SAMP8 mice spent significantly more time in the open arms compared to 9 months old SAMP8 mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by elevated plus maze data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The age-associated increase in disinhibition was prevented by CMS121 and J147.
source: The age-associated increase in disinhibition was prevented by CMS121 and J147.
evidence: This is supported by elevated plus maze data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CMS121 significantly improved the learning of the new location in the Barnes maze reversal phase.
source: However, when tested during the reversal phase, which is more sensitive to deficits in memory and learning, CMS121 significantly improved the learning of the new location (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Barnes maze data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: J147 had no significant effect on learning in the Barnes maze reversal phase.
source: J147 had no significant effect.
evidence: This is based on Barnes maze data analysis.

claim: The transcriptomic aging in old SAMP8 mice is associated with a decline in cognitive function.
source: These data show that the transcriptomic aging in old SAMP8 mice is associated with a decline in cognitive function and that J147 and CMS121 prevent some of this deterioration.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined transcriptomic and behavioral data.

claim: J147 and CMS121 prevent some of the cognitive deterioration in old SAMP8 mice.
source: These data show that the transcriptomic aging in old SAMP8 mice is associated with a decline in cognitive function and that J147 and CMS121 prevent some of this deterioration.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The top KEGG pathway targeted by both aging and CMS121 was oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The top KEGG pathway targeted by both aging and CMS121 was oxidative phosphorylation (OP).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of transcriptomic data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The majority of the DE genes in the oxidative phosphorylation pathway are the same for both aging and CMS121.
source: Moreover, the majority of the DE genes in this pathway are the same for both aging and CMS121 (overlap p-value<0.01, Fisher's Exact Test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of overlapping genes in the oxidative phosphorylation pathway.

claim: The set of DE genes in the OP pathway largely overlapped with those from the Parkinson's disease, AD and Huntington's disease pathways.
source: In addition, the set of DE genes in the OP pathway largely overlapped with those from the Parkinson's disease (PD), AD and Huntington's disease (HD) pathways (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DE genes in the OP, PD, AD and HD pathways included nuclear genes that encode for subunits of complexes I, III and IV of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.
source: These genes included nuclear genes that encode for subunits of complexes I, III and IV of the electron transport chain (ETC) and ATP synthase (complex V) in the mitochondria (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of all ETC and ATP synthase genes went up between 9 and 13 months in the SAMP8 mice and this was prevented by CMS121 and J147.
source: Surprisingly, the expression of all these genes went up between 9 and 13 months in the SAMP8 mice and this was prevented by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The same effect was observed with genes encoded by the mitochondrial DNA.
source: We also observed the same effect with genes encoded by the mitochondrial DNA, which code for proteins necessary for oxidative phosphorylation as well as the tRNA and rRNA necessary for translation in the mitochondria (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap shown in Figure 3D.

claim: One large cluster showed increased changes in gene expression with aging that were prevented by the compounds.
source: We found one large cluster (cluster 2) that showed increased changes in gene expression with aging that were prevented by the compounds (Figure 3E,F), and whose top KEGG pathways were the same as the ones identified in Figure 3A and B, including oxidative phosphorylation, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease.
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3E and pathway analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 are effective in preventing the drift of transcripts associated with mitochondrial proteins.
source: Finally, the transcriptomic drift analysis of the Mitocarta genes shows that both compounds are effective in preventing the drift of transcripts associated with mitochondrial proteins (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomic drift analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA copy number went down with age in SAMP8 mice.
source: We found that mitochondrial DNA copy number went down with age in SAMP8 mice and that only J147 was able to significantly prevent that decrease (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial DNA copy number measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Only J147 was able to significantly prevent the decrease in mitochondrial DNA copy number.
source: We found that mitochondrial DNA copy number went down with age in SAMP8 mice and that only J147 was able to significantly prevent that decrease (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial DNA copy number measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Changes in mitochondrial gene expression correlate with the aging SAMP8 phenotype and are partly prevented by CMS121 and J147.
source: These data show that changes in mitochondrial gene expression correlate with the aging SAMP8 phenotype and are partly prevented by CMS121 and J147.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptomic data presented in Figure 3.

claim: 205 metabolites were significantly altered between 9 and 13 months in the SAMP8 mice.
source: 205 metabolites were significantly altered between 9 and 13 months in the SAMP8 mice and the alterations in some of these metabolites were prevented by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on metabolomic profiling data.

claim: The alterations in some metabolites were prevented by CMS121 and J147.
source: 205 metabolites were significantly altered between 9 and 13 months in the SAMP8 mice and the alterations in some of these metabolites were prevented by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Global suppression of age-related metabolomic changes by the compounds was not as robust as with the transcriptome.
source: Global suppression of age-related metabolomic changes by the compounds was not as robust as with the transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing PCA and drift analyses of metabolomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 showed a partial suppression of the metabolic changes that took place with aging in plasma.
source: Both compounds showed a partial suppression of the changes that took place with aging (Figure 4E,F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by plasma metabolomic data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The metabolic drift analysis showed a significant suppression of plasma metabolic drift by CMS121 and J147.
source: Although not as clear in the PCA (Figure 4D), the metabolic drift analysis showed a significant suppression of plasma metabolic drift by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic drift analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There were increases of 9.51, 7.85, 6.19 and 5.73-fold between 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice in the levels of α-ketoglutarate, succinate, citrate and aconitate, respectively.
source: In fact, increases of 9.51, 7.85, 6.19 and 5.73-fold between 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice in the levels of α-ketoglutarate, succinate, citrate and aconitate, respectively, accounted for the top largest fold changes seen with aging, while there was a 2-fold decrease in acetyl-CoA (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was a 2-fold decrease in acetyl-CoA between 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice.
source: In fact, increases of 9.51, 7.85, 6.19 and 5.73-fold between 9 and 13 months old SAMP8 mice in the levels of α-ketoglutarate, succinate, citrate and aconitate, respectively, accounted for the top largest fold changes seen with aging, while there was a 2-fold decrease in acetyl-CoA (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CMS121 significantly restored the levels of acetyl-CoA, α-ketoglutarate and succinate to 9 months old levels.
source: CMS121 had the largest effect on the metabolites, significantly restoring the levels of acetyl-CoA, α-ketoglutarate and succinate to 9 months old levels (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: J147 preserved the levels of acetyl-CoA.
source: J147 also preserved the levels of acetyl-CoA and, although not statistically significant, it reduced the increases in α-ketoglutarate and succinate seen with aging (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The TCA cycle was among the top pathways preferentially affected by aging.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis with all of the brain metabolites that were significantly altered with aging confirmed that the TCA cycle was among the top pathways preferentially affected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 shared a common top pathway related to the metabolism of acyl carnitines.
source: We then carried out pathway enrichment analysis with the brain metabolites that were altered by the compounds in relation to the 13 months old mice and found that both compounds shared a common top pathway related to the metabolism of acyl carnitines (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Many acyl carnitines were increased by CMS121 and J147 in the old animals.
source: The levels of the different acyl carnitines did not significantly change between 9 and 13 months, but many were increased by CMS121 and J147 in the old animals (Figure 5E), suggesting a shared mechanism of action for the compounds.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The levels of carnitine were significantly decreased in 13 months old mice and rescued by the compounds.
source: The levels of carnitine, which is necessary for the transport of the acyl groups across the mitochondrial inner membrane, were also significantly decreased in 13 months old mice and rescued by the compounds (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The maintenance of mitochondrial gene expression in the brain by CMS121 and J147 is associated with a preservation of key mitochondrial metabolic intermediates.
source: Specifically, these data show that the maintenance of mitochondrial gene expression in the brain by CMS121 and J147 is associated with a preservation of key mitochondrial metabolic intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined transcriptomic and metabolomic data.

claim: The build-up in acyl carnitines with both compounds is suggestive of a mitochondrial target underlying the action of the compounds.
source: Moreover, the build-up in acyl carnitines with both compounds is suggestive of a mitochondrial target underlying the action of the compounds.
evidence: This is an inference from the metabolomic data showing increased acyl carnitines.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is a central metabolite shared by CMS121 and J147.
source: Analysis of the networks generated for each compound showed that acetyl-CoA is a central metabolite shared by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is based on network analysis integrating transcriptomic and metabolomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The decrease in the levels of acetyl-CoA in the brains of 13 months old SAMP8 mice was prevented by CMS121 and J147.
source: Importantly, the decrease in the levels of acetyl-CoA in the brains of 13 months old SAMP8 mice was prevented by CMS121 and J147 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Network analysis of transcriptomic data from cultured neurons treated with CMS121 and J147 identified acetyl-CoA as a central metabolite regulated by both compounds.
source: To provide further support for the central role of acetyl-CoA in the effects of the compounds, network analysis was performed on transcriptomic data from cultured, differentiated rat cortical neurons treated with CMS121 and J147. This analysis also identified acetyl-CoA as a central metabolite regulated by both compounds (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D; random sampling, p=0.01).
evidence: This is based on network analysis of transcriptomic data from primary neurons shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 induced a significant increase in acetyl-CoA in primary cortical neurons.
source: Measurement of acetyl-CoA in these cells confirmed that both compounds induced a significant increase (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurement of acetyl-CoA shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CMS121 and J147 significantly increased acetylation of histone 3 at lysine 9 (H3K9) in primary cortical neurons.
source: In primary cortical neurons, CMS121 and J147 significantly increased acetylation of histone 3 at lysine 9 (H3K9) (Figure 6B), an epitope that has been implicated in memory formation (Fischer et al., 2007; Mews et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H3K9 acetylation has been implicated in memory formation.
source: In primary cortical neurons, CMS121 and J147 significantly increased acetylation of histone 3 at lysine 9 (H3K9) (Figure 6B), an epitope that has been implicated in memory formation (Fischer et al., 2007; Mews et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2007 and Mews et al., 2017.

claim: Acetylation of H3K9 was reduced in the cortex of 13 months old SAMP8 mice relative to 9 months old mice.
source: Importantly, acetylation of H3K9 was reduced in the cortex of 13 months old SAMP8 mice relative to 9 months old mice and both CMS121 and J147 significantly prevented this loss (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 significantly prevented the loss of H3K9 acetylation in SAMP8 mice.
source: Importantly, acetylation of H3K9 was reduced in the cortex of 13 months old SAMP8 mice relative to 9 months old mice and both CMS121 and J147 significantly prevented this loss (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: H3K9 acetylation was increased by CMS121 and J147 in the brains of APPswe/PSEN1dE9 transgenic AD mice.
source: In both cases, acetylation of H3K9 was increased by the compounds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–G.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is a central metabolite that is decreased in the aging brain and increased by CMS121 and J147.
source: These data identify acetyl-CoA as a central metabolite that is decreased in the aging brain and increased by CMS121 and J147, and this increase is associated with acetylation of histone H3 at a site required for memory enhancement.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including metabolomic and Western blot data.

claim: The increase in acetyl-CoA by CMS121 and J147 is associated with acetylation of histone H3 at a site required for memory enhancement.
source: These data identify acetyl-CoA as a central metabolite that is decreased in the aging brain and increased by CMS121 and J147, and this increase is associated with acetylation of histone H3 at a site required for memory enhancement.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined data on acetyl-CoA levels and H3K9 acetylation.

claim: The mechanism of action of J147 is associated with the activation of AMPK.
source: We have recently demonstrated that the mechanism of action of J147 is associated with the activation of AMPK (Goldberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg et al., 2018.

claim: One of the downstream effects of AMPK activation is the inhibition by phosphorylation at serine 79 of ACC1.
source: One of the downstream effects of AMPK activation is the inhibition by phosphorylation at serine 79 of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), an enzyme responsible for the conversion of acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA, which is then utilized to synthesize fatty acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AMPK signaling.

claim: ACC1 is an enzyme responsible for the conversion of acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA.
source: One of the downstream effects of AMPK activation is the inhibition by phosphorylation at serine 79 of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), an enzyme responsible for the conversion of acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA, which is then utilized to synthesize fatty acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ACC1 function.

claim: Malonyl-CoA is utilized to synthesize fatty acids.
source: One of the downstream effects of AMPK activation is the inhibition by phosphorylation at serine 79 of acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1), an enzyme responsible for the conversion of acetyl-CoA into malonyl-CoA, which is then utilized to synthesize fatty acids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fatty acid synthesis.

claim: Inhibition of ACC1 can potentially lead to a build up in acetyl-CoA.
source: Inhibition of ACC1 can thus potentially lead to a build up in acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the role of ACC1 in acetyl-CoA metabolism.

claim: CMS121 and J147 can increase acetyl-CoA in HT22 cells.
source: We first determined that the compounds can increase acetyl-CoA in these cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by direct measurement of acetyl-CoA shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 increased the phosphorylation of ACC1 at serine 79 in HT22 cells and primary neurons.
source: In HT22 cells as well as primary neurons, both CMS121 and J147 increased the phosphorylation of ACC1 at serine 79 (Figure 6F,G; Western blots shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F,G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both CMS121 and J147 increased phospho-ACC1 levels in the brains of the SAMP8 mice.
source: Importantly, both CMS121 and J147 also increased phospho-ACC1 levels in the brains of the SAMP8 mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: ACC1 phosphorylation was elevated with aging in SAMP8 mice.
source: ACC1 phosphorylation was also elevated with aging, and this observation could be associated with a compensatory mechanism.
evidence: This is an observation from the Western blot data with a speculative interpretation.

claim: Inhibition of ACC1 by the compounds was accompanied by a decrease in free fatty acids in primary neurons.
source: In addition, inhibition of ACC1 by the compounds was accompanied by a decrease in free fatty acids in primary neurons (Figure 6I) as well as in the brains (Figure 6J) and plasma (Figure 6K) of old SAMP8 mice.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Inhibition of ACC1 by the compounds was accompanied by a decrease in free fatty acids in the brains of old SAMP8 mice.

claim: Few clinical approaches have focused on treating AD and other dementias by targeting detrimental age-related processes.
source: Despite the observation that old age is the greatest risk factor for AD, few clinical approaches have focused on treating AD and other dementias by targeting detrimental age-related processes that are relevant to disease onset and development.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the current state of AD research.

claim: CMS121 and J147 were able to reduce age-related cognitive dysfunction, even when administered to SAMP8 mice at a late stage of their lives.

claim: CMS121 and J147 share a common mechanism of action that is associated with the maintenance of mitochondrial health in terms of transcriptional stability and metabolism.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the hallmarks of aging.

claim: An acceleration in mitochondrial dysfunction may be responsible for the onset of AD pathology.

claim: Numerous metabolites that did not change with age were directly altered by the compounds.

claim: Acyl carnitines are direct substrates for fatty acid oxidation in mitochondria and a source of acetyl-CoA.
source: Since acyl carnitines are direct substrates for fatty acid oxidation in mitochondria and a source of acetyl-CoA, they further support the conclusion that the compounds have a direct effect on mitochondrial metabolism in the brain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about acyl carnitine metabolism.

claim: CMS121 and J147 suppressed the metabolic drift in the plasma, indicating that the compounds may prevent the aging process at the systemic level.

claim: Mitochondria-related genes were the top pathways affected by aging in SAMP8 mice.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is part of the SAMP8 aging process.
source: Mitochondria-related genes were also the top pathways affected by aging, indicating that mitochondrial dysfunction is part of the SAMP8 aging process.
evidence: This is an inference from the pathway analysis of transcriptomic data.

claim: The increased expression of gene transcripts associated with the ETC with aging is likely a compensatory response to a lack of adequate mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Because a decrease in mitochondrial DNA copy number was found with aging, the increased expression of gene transcripts associated with the ETC with aging is likely a compensatory response to a lack of adequate mitochondrial metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the transcriptomic and mitochondrial DNA copy number data.

claim: Deficits in the respiratory chain and mitochondrial bioenergetics increase as a function of age.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Caldwell et al., 2015 and López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is a key metabolite that bridges glycolysis, fatty acid β-oxidation, fatty acid synthesis and the TCA cycle in the mitochondria.
source: Acetyl-CoA is a key metabolite that bridges glycolysis, fatty acid β-oxidation, fatty acid synthesis and the TCA cycle in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about acetyl-CoA metabolism.

claim: Acetyl-CoA metabolism in the TCA cycle leads to the production of metabolites that are used in other metabolic pathways essential for the proper functioning of the cell.
source: Its metabolism in the TCA cycle leads to the production of metabolites that are used in other metabolic pathways essential for the proper functioning of the cell, including the neurotransmitter acetylcholine which is reduced in forebrain neurons at early stages of the disease (Mufson et al., 2008).

claim: Acetylcholine is reduced in forebrain neurons at early stages of AD.
